raw_text:
# Sacubitril/Valsartan (Angiotensin Receptor-Neprilysin Inhibition) in Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

### Introduction and Mechanism of Action
Heart failure (HF) remains a major global clinical and economic challenge with high morbidity and mortality. Neurohormonal modulation has long been the cornerstone of therapy. A milestone was reached with the introduction of sacubitril/valsartan, the first-in-class angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI) [1]. 

Sacubitril/valsartan represents a unique dual-acting therapeutic class. It combines neprilysin inhibition (via LBQ657, the active metabolite of the prodrug sacubitril) with AT1 receptor blockade (via valsartan). Neprilysin is a zinc-dependent metalloendopeptidase that degrades various endogenous vasoactive peptides, including atrial, B-type, and C-type natriuretic peptides, bradykinin, and adrenomedullin. By inhibiting neprilysin, sacubitril/valsartan increases the concentration of these peptides, which promotes vasodilation, natriuresis, and inhibits cardiac hypertrophy and fibrosis. Simultaneously, valsartan blocks the AT1 receptor, countering the compensatory activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS). Historically, combining neprilysin and ACE inhibition (e.g., omapatrilat in the OVERTURE trial) failed due to an unacceptable risk of life-threatening angioedema [2]. Sacubitril/valsartan avoids this by pairing neprilysin inhibition with an ARB rather than an ACE inhibitor, minimizing dual pathways of bradykinin breakdown.

### Clinical Efficacy in HFrEF
The therapeutic landscape of chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) was redefined by the landmark PARADIGM-HF trial [1]. Comparing sacubitril/valsartan with enalapril in 8,442 patients, the ARNI reduced the primary composite endpoint of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization by 20%, and all-cause mortality by 16% [1]. 

In the acute setting, the PIONEER-HF trial [3] demonstrated that initiating sacubitril/valsartan in hemodynamically stabilized patients hospitalized for acute decompensated HF significantly reduced NT-proBNP levels compared to enalapril. A subsequent analysis [4] showed a significant 42% reduction in serious clinical outcomes (death, rehospitalization, or left ventricular assist device implantation) at 8 weeks. The TRANSITION trial [5] confirmed that initiating therapy either in-hospital (pre-discharge) or early post-discharge is equally safe, tolerable, and feasible. Regarding titration, the TITRATION study [6] highlighted that a conservative 6-week up-titration regimen improved tolerability over a condensed 3-week schedule, particularly in patients with lower baseline systolic blood pressure.

Mechanistic trials have further elucidated these physiological benefits. The PROVE-HF study [7] demonstrated that early NT-proBNP reduction strongly correlates with cardiac reverse remodeling, including increases in left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) and reductions in left ventricular and left atrial volumes. The EVALUATE-HF trial [8] showed significant improvements in central hemodynamics and aortic stiffness compared to enalapril. Furthermore, the PRIME trial [9] reported that sacubitril/valsartan significantly decreases functional mitral regurgitation compared to valsartan.

### Efficacy Across the Ejection Fraction Spectrum
Sacubitril/valsartan's benefits extend beyond HFrEF. The PARAGON-HF trial [10] compared ARNI therapy with valsartan in patients with LVEF ≥45%. Although it narrowly missed statistical significance for the primary composite endpoint, a significant reduction in HF hospitalizations was seen in patients with below-normal LVEF (45%–57%) and in women [10]. The PARAGLIDE-HF trial [11] reinforced these findings in patients with EF >40% and worsening HF, showing superior NT-proBNP reduction and clinical benefit. A pooled participant-level analysis of PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF [12] demonstrated a treatment benefit that spans the entire EF spectrum, tapering only in patients with supranormal ejection fractions. This is consistent with the PARALLAX trial [13], which showed a significant reduction in NT-proBNP in patients with HF and EF >40% compared to individualized standard therapies.

### Other Clinical Scenarios
In patients post-myocardial infarction, the PARADISE-MI trial [14] did not show a significant reduction in CV death or incident HF compared to ramipril, but confirmed the drug's safety in this population. In pediatric patients, the PANORAMA-HF trial [15] demonstrated that sacubitril/valsartan safely reduces NT-proBNP in children with symptomatic systemic left ventricular systolic dysfunction, matching the efficacy of enalapril. However, in patients with severe, advanced chronic HFrEF (NYHA class IV), the LIFE trial [16] showed that sacubitril/valsartan was not superior to valsartan in reducing NT-proBNP or clinical events, though tolerability was comparable.

### Guidelines, Practical Implementation, and Cardiorenal Protection
Reflecting this evidence, the 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guidelines [17] designate ARNI as a Class 1 recommendation in chronic HFrEF. The 2021 ESC guidelines [18] and the 2023 Focused Update [19] also recommend ARNI as first-line therapy for HFrEF and suggest consideration for HFmrEF and HFpEF. To maximize survival, modern sequencing algorithms emphasize the rapid, concurrent initiation of the four foundational pillars [20].

In terms of cardiorenal safety, sacubitril/valsartan is highly protective. A subanalysis of PARADIGM-HF by Damman et al. [21] revealed a slower decline in eGFR with sacubitril/valsartan compared to enalapril. The UK-HARP-III trial [22] proved that ARNI is as safe and effective on GFR as irbesartan in moderate-to-severe chronic kidney disease while further lowering blood pressure. Mc Causland et al.'s pooled spectrum analysis [23] confirmed consistent renal preservation across all ejection fractions. Additionally, sacubitril/valsartan improves glycemic control, as shown by Seferovic et al. [24] who reported a significant reduction in HbA1c in patients with diabetes. Regarding electrolytes, Desai et al. [25] and Ferreira et al. [26] reported that sacubitril/valsartan reduces the risk of severe hyperkalemia compared to enalapril, even in patients taking mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs).

Lastly, to avoid angioedema [27], a 36-hour washout period is mandatory when transitioning from an ACE inhibitor. Real-world pharmacovigilance analyses [28] confirm that the risk of angioedema is low but elevated when the washout is omitted. Overall, sacubitril/valsartan represents a major breakthrough, preventing overall clinical progression [29] and improving patient-reported health-related quality of life [30].
